sections.html: Triportheus nematurus becomes about 20 cm long. It is an omnivore and, as far as is known, a free spawner without brood care.

The genus Triportheus currently contains 16 species that inhabit all major river systems of South America. Members of the genus are imported from Paraguay, where two species occur: T. nematurus and T. pantanensis. The two can only be told apart for sure by counting the gill rakers on the first gill arch, which cannot be done in live fish. T. pantanensis is more deep-bodied than T. nematurus, although the measurements expressing this overlap to a degree. The fish imported are assumed to be T. nematurus, which is supported by the counts of the lateral scale row and details of the coloration.

As a subtropical species it tolerates a relatively wide temperature range, between 16°C (rarely even less) and 28°C during the season. Regarding water chemistry these fish are undemanding; any drinking water is suitable.

Triportheus are omnivores; in nature, insects that fall into the water are an important part of their diet. In the aquarium they take every usual ornamental fish food. Big specimens become dangerous even for small fish of mouth-size.

Like all species of Triportheus it has mighty pectoral muscles. The tetras, much like the hatchetfishes, jump out of the water when hunted by a predator and "fly" for a short distance. Its feeding is also interesting: in contrast to most other tetras, which are pickers, Triportheus slurps the water surface with many fast openings of the mouth and swirls small food particles into the mouth.

Adult narrow hatchetfishes have fold-out skin flaps on their lower lip, with which they can survive in oxygen-poor waters. In such cases the animals, which live close to the surface anyway, swim just below the water surface and swirl the air with the uppermost layer of water with rapid mouth movements. The skin lobes absorb the oxygen that gets into the water in a way usable for the fish.
Breeding in the aquarium has not yet been reported; it has probably never been tried. As far as is known the animals are free spawners without brood care.
